summary: Erik Hanchett opens by introducing himself as a senior developer advocate at AWS and announces five methods to reduce token costs when creating agents. The first technique is caching the system prompt. Using AWS Strands agents as the demonstration framework, he shows that setting a cache prompt flag sends the full system prompt only on the first call, with subsequent calls using a reduced cached version. Tool prompts and messages can also be cached. The second technique is model routing based on difficulty. Hanchett recommends using cheaper models such as Claude Haiku for simpler tasks and more capable models like Claude Sonnet for difficult ones, potentially even using a cheap model to decide which model to route to. The third technique is offloading tool results. Large tool results can be stored locally or in the cloud and summarized, preventing them from being re-sent into the context on every agent loop iteration. Strands agents offers additional APIs for this. The fourth technique is capping tool loops. Without a maximum iteration setting, agents may call tools repeatedly or enter infinite loops, consuming excessive tokens. He recommends using observability tools before deployment to inspect how long each tool call takes and how many times it loops, then iterating for efficiency. The fifth technique is trimming conversation history in multi-turn agents. Strands agents provides a sliding window conversation manager that sends only the last N messages, configurable to any number. The trade-off is losing early message history, which can be mitigated by summarizing the history and injecting that summary into the context window. He concludes by reiterating all five points and directing listeners to his blog at programwitheric.com and social media handle EricCH for further discussion.

takeaways: Cache system prompts so the full prompt is sent only on the first call, reducing tokens on subsequent calls; tool prompts and messages can also be cached.
Route tasks by difficulty—use cheaper models like Claude Haiku for simple tasks and frontier models like Claude Sonnet only for complex ones.
Offload and summarize large tool results so they are not re-sent into the context on every agent loop iteration.
Cap tool loop iterations to prevent runaway or infinite loops that consume excessive tokens.
Use a sliding window conversation manager to trim history in multi-turn agents, summarizing older history to preserve context.
Run observability tools before deployment to measure tool call duration and loop counts, then iterate for efficiency.
All five techniques require only small code changes and do not require changing prompts or switching models.

Understanding of how to use observability to diagnose token waste in tool calls
Knowledge of trade-offs when trimming conversation history and how to mitigate them

sections.summary: Erik Hanchett introduces himself as a senior developer advocate at AWS and announces five ways to reduce token costs when creating agents.

sections.title: Cache the System Prompt
sections.summary: Demonstrates using Strands agents to cache the system prompt so the full prompt is sent only on the first call and subsequent calls use a reduced cached version. Tool prompts and messages can also be cached.

sections.title: Route by Difficulty
sections.summary: Recommends routing tasks to models based on difficulty, using cheaper models like Claude Haiku for simple tasks and Claude Sonnet for difficult ones, potentially using a cheap model to decide routing.

sections.title: Offload Tool Results
sections.summary: Shows how to store large tool results locally or in the cloud and summarize them, preventing the full result from being re-sent into context on every agent loop iteration. Strands agents offers APIs for this.

sections.title: Cap Tool Loops
sections.summary: Advises setting a max iterations to prevent tools from being called repeatedly or entering infinite loops. Recommends using observability tools before deployment to inspect tool call duration and loop counts.

sections.title: Trim Conversation History
sections.summary: Introduces Strands agents' sliding window conversation manager that sends only the last N messages. Trade-off is losing early history, mitigated by summarizing older history into the context window.

sections.title: Conclusion and Contact
sections.summary: Recaps all five techniques and provides contact information: LinkedIn at Eric Hanchett, blog at programwitheric.com, and social media at EricCH.

demonstrations: Code example using AWS Strands agents with cache prompt set to default for system prompt caching
Code example showing model routing with if statements for difficulty-based model selection
Code example for offloading and summarizing large tool results in Strands agents
Sliding window conversation manager in Strands agents configured to look back at last 10 messages
limitations: Sliding window trimming loses early message history from the conversation context
Tool result offloading and history trimming are manual techniques requiring additional summarization logic
Code shown is pseudo code rather than production-ready implementations
quantitativeClaims: Sliding window example looks back at the last 10 messages
Uncapped tool loops could run 10, 20 times or enter an infinite loop
Full conversation history can eat through hundreds if not thousands of tokens per call
